Abstract
    

For integers n≥s≥2n\geq s\geq 2, let e⁡(n,s)e(n,s) be the maximum size of a family
ℱ⊆2[n]\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{[n]} with no ss pairwise disjoint members.
The problem of determining e⁡(n,s)e(n,s) is closely related to its uniform
counterpart, the Erdős Matching Conjecture.
Frankl and Kupavskii conjectured an exact formula for e⁡((m+1)​s−ℓ,s)e((m+1)s-\ell,s) when 1≤ℓ≤⌈s/2⌉1\leq\ell\leq\lceil s/2\rceil.
We prove that for every fixed m≥3m\geq 3 and sufficiently large ss, the extremal families for e⁡((m+1)​s−ℓ,s)e((m+1)s-\ell,s) are
    




P⁡(m,s,ℓ,L)≔{A⊆[n]:|A|+|A∩L|≥m+1}​ for some L with ​|L|=ℓ−1P(m,s,\ell;L)\coloneqq\{A\subseteq[n]\colon|A|+|A\cap L|\geq m+1\}\text{ for some $L$ with }|L|=\ell-1


    

when 1≤ℓ≤(m+12​m+1−o⁡(1))​s1\leq\ell\leq(\frac{m+1}{2m+1}-o(1))s.
In particular, this confirms the Frankl–Kupavskii conjecture for every
fixed m≥3m\geq 3 and all sufficiently large ss.
For m=3m=3 and sufficiently large ss, we determine the exact range of ℓ\ell for which P⁡(3,s,ℓ,L)P(3,s,\ell;L) is extremal, generalizing a theorem of Kupavskii and Sokolov.
  




1 Introduction




Let [n]≔{1,2,…,n}[n]\coloneqq\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
A family is a collection of sets.
For a set XX and an integer kk, we write (Xk)\binom{X}{k} for the family of
all kk-element subsets of XX, and we write
(X≥k)≔⋃i≥k(Xi)\binom{X}{\geq k}\coloneqq\bigcup_{i\geq k}\binom{X}{i}.
Given an integer nn, we also write (n≥k)\binom{n}{\geq k} for ∑i=kn(ni)\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i}.
A matching in a family is a collection of pairwise disjoint sets.
An ss-matching is a matching of size ss.
Given a family ℱ\mathcal{F}, its matching number ν⁡(ℱ)\nu(\mathcal{F}) is the size of a
largest matching contained in ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Extremal problems concerning matching numbers in set systems date back to the classical work of Erdős in the 1960s.
One of the representative results is the classical Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem [4].
Erdős [2] proposed the following problem: determining the largest possible size of a kk-uniform family that contains no given number of
pairwise disjoint members.
This problem is now known as the Erdős Matching Conjecture.
